summary: Earth Systems Trend Detective is a web platform that turns a plain-language question about a local place into a statistically tested finding built on NASA Earth-observation data. The user clicks their region on a map of Kyrgyzstan, picks Water, Land or Air, chooses an object a lake, a glacier, a river — and selects a variable described in plain language rather than by satellite product code. The platform pulls the matching record through NASA APIs, reduces it to one value per year, and runs the Mann–Kendall test with a Theil–Sen slope to establish whether the trend is real or just noise. An AI layer, fine-tuned on peer-reviewed climate research and locked to the series on screen, then explains in human language what changed, where, when and by how much — and ends by asking the user what they think connects it. We use NASA GISS GISTEMP to show which global trend the local change lines up with, with a focus on the water resources of Kyrgyzstan, alongside land aridity and regional air quality. Existing tools stop where science begins: Giovanni builds the time series but runs no significance test, and KNMI Climate Explorer does the statistics but is built for climatologists. We close that gap, so a student  not only a climate scientist  can determine what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant.
details:
.Existing tools stop exactly where science begins: Giovanni builds the time series and hands over a CSV with no significance test; KNMI Climate Explorer does the statistics but is built for climatologists. We close that gap in one flow.Every result carries its provenance: observation or model, years present and missing, data latency, and a dataset citation ready to paste into a paper.Null results are usable. When nothing is significant we say so plainly and estimate how many more years of observation would be needed — which the challenge brief explicitly asks for

We make the complex simple, and make science feel worth doing.

A satellite product code becomes one sentence a fifteen-year-old understands. A p-value becomes “the chance this is coincidence is under one percent.” A slope becomes “280 football pitches of new water above a toxic tailings pond.”

The AI ends its explanation by asking the user what they think connects two trends, which turns a reader of charts into an investigator. Our measure of success is not page views — it is whether a student finishes an investigation they started themselves. The primary beneficiaries are school and university students across Central Asia who must produce real research and currently have no usable data path, plus teachers, journalists and local administrations who need a number they can cite.


  • NASA Giovanni, AppEEARS (REST API), GES DISC Hydrology Time Series, Landsat 5/7/8/9, MODIS (snow cover, land surface temperature), GPM precipitation, NASA GISS GISTEMP v4, NOAA Climate Data Online. Python (Mann–Kendall, seasonal and autocorrelation-corrected variants, Theil–Sen), NumPy, rasterio, FastAPI. A pre-computed Parquet data cube for Kyrgyzstan, so demonstrations never wait on a live archive query. a fine-tuned qwen 3.5 model, constrained by retrieval over a curated corpus of peer-reviewed climate papers and by the displayed series. Claude was used during development for literature synthesis, code scaffolding, adversarial critique of our own method, and the pitch deck. React, Leaflet.standard laptops; model fine-tuning on a rented GPU instanceFour things no existing tool combines: not by product code — the step every NASA tool assumes you have already taken. so significance is part of the answer rather than a separate project in Python. grounded in published research, locked to the chart in front of the user, and obliged to end every verdict with what this result does not prove.It does not deliver a conclusion; it hands the case to the user. Small, fast-forming glacial lakes are the most dangerous and the hardest to see on a long record: a lake of 0.02 km² is only about 22 Landsat pixels. Where coverage is too thin, the tool rather than returning a confident wrong number. Reservoir levels and regulated river reaches are driven by dam operation, not climate. Those objects carry a warning label, so a user does not publish an energy-policy signal as a climate finding. GLDAS and MERRA-2 are model output, not orbital measurement. Where we use them, the interface says so.The user clicks an administrative region, because that is how people think; the data behind it is aggregated by watershed, because that is how water works. Our method follows published practice in satellite time-series trend detection, including the work of James G. Acker and colleagues at NASA GES DISC, whose paper on time-series trend analysis and significance testing the challenge itself lists as a resource; plus regional research on Tien Shan glacier retreat and glacial lake evolution (Janský et al. 2009; Engel et al. 2012; Narama et al. 2010; Zheng et al. 2019; Veh et al. 2023).
